*Zendisch*de{}|Proper noun}langname)}#Zend language}#}'''1834''',Jacob Grimm,''Deutsche Mythologie'' (4th edition - 1875),Vol. 1 p. 12 (translation from James Steven Stallybrass ''Teutonic Mythology'')}#}:2Zu gott hat man längst das pers. khodâ (Bopp vrgl. gramm. s. 35) gehalten. wenn dieses,wie aufgestellt worden ist,durch eine starke verkürzung aus dem '''zendischen''' qvadâta (a se datus,increatus,sanskr. svadâta) vgl. Dêvadatta Θεόδοτος,Mitradatta  ‛Ηλιόδοτος,Srîdatta hervorgieng,so wäre unser deutsches wort ursprünglich zusammensetzung und von treffendem sinn,wie denn auch die Serben gott als samozazdani boshe,selbsterschaffner gott! anreden.+3The word God has long been compared with the Pers. khodâ (Bopp,comp. gram.,p. 35). If the latter be,as has been supposed,a violent contraction of the '''Zend''' qvadâta (a se datus,increatus,Sanskr. svadâta,conf. Dêvadatta Θεόδοτος,Mitradatta ‛Ηλιόδοτος,Srîdatta) then our Teutonic word must have been originally a compound,and one with a very apt meaning,as the Servians also address God as samozazdâni bôzhe ! self-created God ;

*Zettel*de{}ein ''Zettel''.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈt͡sɛtl̩}Zet+tel|Etymology 1}Early Modern High German zeddel,zedel,from Middle High German zedele,from Middle High German zedel,a loan from Italian cedola,from German cedula,from Latin schedula,the diminutive of from Latin scheda,from Latin tstrip of papyrus ultimately from Ancient Greek tsplinter,fragment. Cognate to from Low German Zeddel,Palatine from Rhine Franconian Zeddel,from English schedule.}The spelling with ''-tt-'' was found from the 15th century in Upper German; the spelling with ''-dd-'' persisted until the 19th century,primarily in authors from Central or Northern Germany. Luther mostly writes ''zedel'',Goethe alternates between ''zeddel'' and ''zettel''. The (now obsolete) spelling variant ''zettul'' is influenced by from French cédule.}Occasional weak inflection was found in Middle High German and persisted into the 18th century. The original feminine gender was retained until Luther's time,but occasional masculine or neuter gender was found by the late Middle High German period. The masculine gender has predominated since the 19th century.|Alternative forms}zedel}zeddel}ziddel}zöttel}zättel}zettul}Zeddel}Zettul|Noun}(mask.,diminituve:[Zettelchen])}#a small or loose piece of paper,slip}#}Zettel der schutzengel ... sträuet etliche '''zettele''' nider,darauf schöne sprüch aus heiliger schrift wider die hoffart}•the guardian angel scatters a number of loose pages from above,on which are fine sayings from the holy writ against the sin of pride}#note,message,letter}#}'''1511''',Albrecht von Eyb,''Spiegel der Sitten'',Augsburg,https://books.google.ch/books?idsaNJAAAAcAAJ 92v. *Zibbe*de{}wikipedia:langde|Alternative forms}rare,dialectal,archaic|Etymology}19th century. Probably from or related to from Proto-West Germanic tbitch,female dog,whence also from Middle Low German tēve,from Middle Low German tiffe,from Middle Dutch tēve (13th c.,modern from Dutch teef),from Old English tife.}While the 19th-century attestation is surely belated,the total lack of medieval evidence and the fact that the word is native almost exclusively in East Central German,thus outside the original from Old High German - territory,make its inheritedness from German nocap1. *Ziege*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German zige,from Old High German ziga,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆tigā.  was originally found in Franconian dialects alongside otherwise exclusive Geiß. In Middle High German times,it established itself in the colonial dialects (East Central German) and also conquered vast areas of Low German,where the borrowing from Middle Low German sēge was predominant since at least the 15th century (due to a virtual lack of domestic goat breeding). During the same time,curiously,was widely lost in West Central German and Upper Franconian,its original provenance. Its eventual victory in the standard language was reinforced by its use in Luther’s Bible.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈt͡siːɡə/}De-Ziege.OGG}Ⓓ7/73/De-Ziege2.ogg}Zie+ge|Noun}(fem.)}#goat}•synononym [Geiß (regional)<g:f)],[Hippe (regional)]}#informal a stupid,stubborn person (usually female)}•synononym Zicke|Usage notes}The singular refers principally to female goats,though it might also be used for male ones. The plural is entirely neutral with regard to natural gender.}The female gender may be specified by means of the word Zicke,which is uncommon in literary German,however.|Derived terms}alte Ziegen lecken auch gern Salz}Ziegenbart,Ziegenbock,Ziegenfell,Ziegenficker,Ziegenkäse,Ziegenmilch,Ziegenstall}Angoraziege,Bergziege,Hausziege,Milchziege,Schneeziege,Wildziege,Zimtziege|See also}Bock}Geißbock}Zicke

*Zigeuner*de{}|Etymology}from Middle High German Cigäwnär (mentioning,1420s),compare from Middle High German Zeginer and from Middle High German Ziginer (15th century).}Most likely from a from German - term meaning "untouchable"; compare the Modern Greek designations from Greek Τσιγγάνοι,from Greek Αθίγγανοι. Cognate to from Hungarian cigány and terms borrowed from it such as from English tzigane,from Portuguese cigano,from French tzigane,from Romanian țigan,and from Russian цыга́н; see those entries for other cognates and for more information.}The extended senses derive from racist and/or Romantic stereotypes of the Roma.|Pronunciation}IPA:/t͡siˈɡɔɪ̯nɐ/}Ⓓf/fc/De-Zigeuner.ogg|Noun}(mask.)}#sometimes Gypsy,member of the Roma,Romani person}#sometimes member of any of several other nomadic minorities}#offensive disorderly,lazy or dodgy person}#offensive bohemian; unconventional or nonconformist artist or writer|Usage notes}The Central Council of German Sinti and Roma rejects the use of "Zigeuner" as a designation for the Roma,regarding it as racist and as having been discredited by the Nazis' use of it. Nonetheless,some Romani individuals continue to use the term.|Synonyms}sense:gypsy Rotationseuropäer}in plural Sinti und Roma,Roma und Sinti,Roma|Hyponyms}Zigeunerfrau}Zigeunerjunge}Zigeunerkind}Zigeunermädchen}Zigeunermann}Zigeunerweib|Derived terms}Zigeunerapfel}Zigeunerart}Zigeunerbande}Zigeunerfamilienlager,Zigeuner-Familienlager}zigeunerhaft}Zigeunergecko}Zigeunerglocke}Zigeunerglocken}Zigeunerhahn}Zigeunerhuhn}zigeunerisch}Zigeunerjazz}Zigeunerkapelle}Zigeunerklößchen}Zigeunerklösschen}Zigeunerkraut}Zigeunerlager}Zigeunerlauch}Zigeunerleben}Zigeunerleute}Zigeunermusik}zigeunern}Zigeunerpack}Zigeunerpilz}Zigeunerprimas}Zigeunersauce}Zigeunerschnitzel}Zigeunersoße}Zigeunersosse}Zigeunerschnitzel}Zigeunersprache}Zigeunerstamm}Zigeunertonalität}Zigeunertonleiter}Zigeunervolk}Zigeunerware}Zigeunerweise}Zigeunerwagen}Zigeunerwesen}Zigeunerwirtschaft}Zigeunerwurz

Verlag,page 19:}#}:Die eigenen '''Zimmer''' hatten sich die Enkel nach persönlichem Geschmack eingerichtet.+The grandchildren had furnished their own '''rooms''' according to their personal taste.|Usage notes}is used of the rooms in a private dwelling,excluding cellar and loft unless they are furnished and used as a part of the dwelling,and usually also excluding passages,kitchens,larders,toilets,utility rooms,and the like (though a private bathroom is called Badezimmer).}In collectively used dwellings such as hotels,shelters,or hospitals,is used chiefly of those rooms that are private to a small number of people (one to circa ten). *Zirkel*de{}''' (monogram),comprised of E,F,V.}wp:Zirkel (Studentenverbindung)|Etymology}From Middle High German zirkel,from Old High German zirkil,from Latin tpair of compasses,from Ancient Greek κίρκινος. The Old High German ''-il'' is due to either alteration after the Germanic tool suffix from Proto-Germanic ⋆-ilaz,or confluence with from Latin tcircle; the ''-k-'' speaks in favour of the latter explanation. The sense “circle”,which appears in Middle High German,is at any rate borrowed from Latin circulus. Both Latin words ultimately go back to from Ancient Greek κίρκος.|Pronunciation}IPA:-kəl}Ⓓ7/7b/De-Zirkel.ogg|Noun}(mask.)}#pair of compasses,compass gloss:device to draw circles}#rare circle gloss:geometrical figure}•synononym Kreis<qq:much more common)}#figurative circle gloss:group of persons with a common interest}•synononym Kreis}#monogram,(English) of a student society.|Derived terms}zirkeln,zirkulär,zirkulieren

*zumindest*de{}|Etymology}[zu]+[mindest]|Pronunciation}IPA:/t͡suˈmɪndəst/}Ⓓ6/64/De-zumindest.ogg|Adverb}#at least}•synononym [[immerhin],[mindestens]],[wenigstens]}•Du brauchst '''zumindest''' einen Führerschein,um Auto zu fahren.}•Geleistet hast du nichts,aber '''zumindest''' bist du überhaupt gekommen.|Usage notes}Although ''zumindest'' and mindestens can often be used interchangeably,there is a tendency to distinguish them. ''Mindestens'' is preferred when there is an actual ranking,particularly one involving numbers,whereas ''zumindest'' is used otherwise.}In the examples above,''mindestens'' could be used alternatively in the first sentence,whereas it would sound awkward in the second. The difference is that sentence 2 does not express a requirement or lower limit but simply the insufficiency of the addressed person’s efforts.

*zusammen*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German together,from Old High German together. From zu+t1to+sammen++t2together (in Modern German,sammen is only found in compounds),from Proto-Germanic together,from Proto-Indo-European together,one. Cognate with from Middle English together. Related to obsolete from Samaritan Aramaic together,whose earlier form was from English samen.}from Dutch together has been formed in a similar fashion,with its contracted form being from Dutch samen and its ancestral form from Middle Dutch tsamen. Also cognate with from Scots together,from Danish together,from Swedish together.|Pronunciation}IPA:aastandard}IPA:aacolloquial variant}IPA:aaBavaria,Austria}IPA:aacolloquial in Bavaria,Austria}Ⓓ6/6d/De-zusammen.ogg}zu+sam+men|Adverb}#together,jointly}•Antonym:getrennt}•'''Zusammen''' bilden wir ein gutes Team.}•'''Together''' we make a good team.}#}'''1903''',w:Fanny zu Reventlow,''Ellen Olestjerne'',in ''Franziska Gräfin zu Reventlow:Gesammelte Werke'',Albert Langen,page 526:}#}:Trotz all dieser Bitternisse war es noch ein wunderbar schöner Sommer,den die drei Freunde '''zusammen''' verlebten.+Despite all these bitter feelings,it was yet a wonderfully beautiful summer,which the three friends spent together.|Usage notes}Unlike the English "together",''zusammen'' does not imply "with me" in an invitation. In this situation one might use ''mit mir'' instead.|Synonyms}all restricted to certain contexts}beieinander}gemeinsam}miteinander}vereint}zueinander|Derived terms}see zusammen-}sich *zwei*Alemannic German}ain|Alternative forms}zwëi|Etymology}From Middle High German zwei,from Old High German zwei (neuter of from Old High German zwēne).}Cognate with from German zwei,from Dutch twee,from English two,from Icelandic tveir.|Number}zwei:}#two}German}number box:de|Alternative forms}zwey|Etymology}From Middle High German zwei,from Old High German zwei (neuter of from Old High German zwēne).}Compare from Dutch twee,from English two,from English twain. In Old High German,and still today in some dialects,distinct forms are used for the three grammatical genders. ''Zwei'' was originally the neuter form,now used for all genders. The Old High German masculine from Old High German zwēne is found back in early modern from German zween; the feminine from Old High German zwō lives on in the variant zwo (but now without any gender distinction).|Pronunciation}IPA:t͡sʋaɪ̯}Ⓓ2/27/De-zwei.ogg}Ⓓ2/2e/De-zwei2.ogg}IPA:q1regionally}Rhymes:aɪ̯|Numeral}zwei:}#cardinal two gloss:numerical value represented by the Arabic numeral 2; or ''describing a set with two components''}•synononym zwo|Coordinate terms}de-cardinals|Derived terms}Zweiklang}Zweiweg- (Gleichrichter)|See also}Silesian ees,zwee,drei,vier,fimf,sechs,siem,acht,neun,zahn,elf,zwelf

*ᛉ*de{},Germany.|Etymology}From the interpretation as Lebensrune.|Symbol}from German symbol}#obsolete born (replacing})}•from German ᛦ
*ᛦ*de{},Germany.}.|Etymology}From the interpretation as Todesrune.|Symbol}ᛦ:}#obsolete died,dead (replacing †)}•ᛉ|Usage notes}The rune is part of the w:Armanen runes,which are based on the Younger Futhark. The visual representation of the rune in the original publication is closer to ⟨ᛣ⟩,with straight arms to mirror ⟨ᛉ⟩,but this denotes a different letter,m+:calc IPAchar:/k/,and not ''yr''. There is currently no specific codepoint in Unicode for straight-armed ''yr'' as opposed to curved-armed ''yr'',so both are conventionally encoded as ⟨ᛦ⟩. It should be noted that the distinction between round and straight runes is purely graphemic,and not historically something that distinguishes one runic script from another.

à la*a la*de{}|Etymology}Borrowed fr.|Preposition}from German preposition}#à la
Ä*A*de{}|Alternative forms}lowercase|Etymology}letter From Alemannic from Middle High German aͤ,a representation of secondary umlaut æ. In Early Modern German,the letter spread to Central German,which did not have a special phoneme for secondary umlaut. Therefore,was seen there as a marker of umlaut as such,and was used analogously.}sound from Middle High German - distinguished up to five stressed e-vowels:æ,ɛ,ɛː,e,eː. Through open-syllable lengthening,mergers,and analogy,this system was not just reduced but entirely altered. 19th-century Standard German generally retained only one short vowel,but distinguished ɛː from eː. All long ⟨ä⟩s were by then usually pronounced ɛː,while ⟨e⟩ was ɛː in some words,eː in others. The choice between these,however,varied greatly from region to region,and was entirely absent in many Low German areas. Theodor Siebs therefore (consistently but rather arbitrarily) restricted ɛː to the spelling ⟨ä⟩ in his codification of stage and broadcasting German. Unintendedly,this reinforced the tendency towards total merger as the dialectal systems of distinction were disturbed.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˌaː ˈʊmlaʊ̯t/letter name}Ⓓ2/2e/De-%C3%84.ogg}IPA:/ɛ/short phoneme}IPA:eː long phoneme}The distinction between long IPAchar:/ɛː/and IPAchar:/eː/is maintained in some regions,including Switzerland and most of western Germany. In many other regions the two are merged in normal speech,though speakers may nevertheless distinguish them in individual words (such as conditional forms of strong verbs,e.g.,gäbe) and in enunciation. This usually also includes the monosyllabic pronunciation of the letter name ⟨Ä⟩ itself.}Rhymes:eː one pronunciation}E one pronunciation|Letter}(neut.,genitive:Äs,plural:[Äs])}#ng:A

The nine of spades is a negative card in tarot card reading,traditionally associated with death.}The form  suggests origin in East Central German,where such nominalized numerals in  are common,perhaps specifically Berlin. Altsächsisch*Altsachsisch*de{}wikipedia:langde|Etymology}[[[alt]+[Sächsisch]]+[gloss1old]]+[gloss2Saxon] or substantivisation of altsächsisch|Pronunciation}Ⓓe/e8/De-Alts%C3%A4chsisch.ogg|Proper noun}langname)}#Old Saxon (the Old Saxon language)}•synononym [[altsächsische Sprache],[Altniederdeutsch]],[altniederdeutsche Sprache]}#}'''2003''',Stefan Sonderegger,''Althochdeutsche Sprache und Literatur:Eine Einführung in das älteste Deutsch:Darstellung und Grammatik'',3rd ed. äugen*augen*de{}|Alternative forms}obsolete|Etymology}Formally from Middle High German öugen,from Middle High German ougen,from Old High German ougen,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆augijan,all meaning “to show,let see”. -en. The modern sense “to look” seems to be of northern origin,being first attested in from Middle Low German ö̂gen,from Middle Dutch ôgen (both 15th century). It only became common in standard German in the 19th century. There may also have been influence by äugeln,which had this sense already in Middle High German.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈɔʏ̯ɡən/}Eugen|Verb}de-verb}#intransitive to look in a searching or cautious way (typically said of animals or of shy,anxious or curious persons)}•Sie '''äugte''' ängstlich um die Ecke.}•She '''peered''' fearfully around the corner.}•Das Baby '''äugte''' neugierig umher.}•The baby '''peered''' around curiously.}#transitive to show,allow to see|Derived terms}beäugen}äugeln

Befähigung zum Richteramt*Befahigung zum Richteramt*de{}|Noun}(fem.)}#Germany the status of a person who qualifies for practice as an attorney,state attorney,or judge due to either having completed legal education with the successful first and second state examinations (Volljurist) or being a professor ordinarius of law (which only requires the first state examination,alone however empirically rare for a professor of law). Such persons also qualify for all levels of public administration as civil servants in the same fashion as those master's level graduates who have completed preparatory service (Referendariat) specific to public administration.

belämmert*belammert*de{}|Alternative forms}belemmert|Etymology}Past participle of the rarer verb belämmern or belemmern,from Middle Low German belemmeren. The verb pertains to lahm and is cognate with from Dutch to hamper. The semantic development of the adjective in German is,at least in part,due to association with Lamm (“lamb”,plural Lämmer),a supposedly naïve or stupid animal. Hence also the folketymological reform spelling with ''-ä-''.|Pronunciation}IPA:/bəˈlɛmɐt/}Ⓓ3/33/De-bel%C3%A4mmert.ogg|Participle}belämmert:}#past participle of [belämmern]|Adjective}#perplexed; in a sudden state of confusion (e.g. through a lack of concentration,or shock)}•Könnten Sie das bitte noch mal wiederholen? betrügen*betrugen*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:-ɡən}Ⓓ5/52/De-betr%C3%BCgen.ogg|Etymology 1}from Proto-Indo-European iddeceive}From Middle High German betriegen,from Old High German bitriogan,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆bidreugan. Equivalent to be+trügen. The modern ''-ü-'' in this verb chiefly follows the development in the rhyming word lügen. It was reinforced by the noun Betrug and by the 2nd and 3rd person-singular forms (as in  itself,which compare).|Verb}betrügen(betrog,betrogen,betröge)}#transitive to deceive (usually deliberately)}•synononym [[[täuschen],[belügen]],[hintergehen]],[vorspielen]}•Sie '''betrügt''' dich mit ihrer falschen Fürsorge.}•She '''deceives''' you with her disingenuous care for you.}•Du '''betrügst''' dich,wenn du noch auf Besserung hoffst.}•You '''deceive''' yourself if you still hope for improvement.}#transitive to defraud; to perform an act of fraud against; to swindle}•synononym [[[über den Tisch ziehen],[übers Ohr hauen]],[neppen]],[übervorteilen]}•Er hat die Firma um mehrere tausend Euro '''betrogen'''.}•He '''defrauded''' the company of several thousands of euros.}•Diese Straßenhändler '''betrügen''',wo sie nur können.}•These street hawkers '''swindle''' whenever they get the chance.}#transitive to betray (sexually or romantically); to cheat on}•synononym fremdgehen}•Er hat seine Frau mit einer Arbeitskollegin '''betrogen'''.}•He '''cheated on''' his wife with one of his coworkers.}•Es ist völliger Unsinn,dass alle Männer '''betrügen''' würden.}•It's complete nonsense to say that all men '''cheat'''.}#intransitive to cheat}•synononym [[mogeln],[schummeln]],[pfuschen]}•Sie hat nur gewonnen,weil sie '''betrogen''' hat.}•She only won because she '''cheated'''.|Alternative forms}obsolete|Derived terms}Betrügen}Betrüger}Betrügung|Etymology 2}See the lemma.|Verb}#
